title: By the charcoal fire (John 18:12–27)
hookLine: Peter warms himself and denies him

lines: OUTSIDE: A FIRE IN THE COURTYARD.
cards: Two scenes are happening at once tonight, and John cuts between them like a film editor. Inside, Jesus is questioned by Annas, father-in-law of the high priest Caiaphas. Outside, in the courtyard, it's cold.
Servants and officers have built a fire, hands out to the warmth. And among them stands Peter. Earlier tonight he said he would lay down his life for Jesus.
Then he swung a sword in the garden. Now he's at a fire, trying to look like he belongs.

teach.h: A FIRE OF COALS, FOR IT WAS COLD.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "And the servants and officers stood there, who had made a fire of coals; for it was cold: and they warmed themselves: and Peter stood with them, and warmed himself."
Three times, Peter is asked. First the girl who keeps the door: "Art not thou also one of this man's disciples? He saith, I am not." Then someone at the fire asks the same, and again: I am not.
Then a relative of Malchus, the man whose ear Peter cut off: "Did not I see thee in the garden with him?" Peter denied again, "and immediately the cock crew." Put this beside yesterday.
In the garden, Jesus said, ego eimi, I am. At the fire, Peter says, ouk eimi, I am not. John sets them almost side by side.
One steps forward; one steps back into the crowd.

teach.h: I AM, INSIDE; I AM NOT, OUTSIDE.
teach.b: And inside, at the same time, Jesus tells the high priest: I spoke openly to the world; ask the people who heard me. He's naming witnesses, while one of his own disciples stands outside saying he isn't one.

teach.h: ANTHRAKIA: A WORD THAT COMES BACK.
teach.b: The Greek word for this charcoal fire is anthrakia. John will use that word for a fire once more, much later. Hold on to it.
Readers have long found Peter's denial painful and strangely hopeful at once. Painful because it's so ordinary: he isn't tortured, just asked by a doorkeeper.

teach.h: AND PETER STOOD WITH THEM, AND WARMED HIMSELF.
teach.b: Hopeful because the church remembers this same Peter, later on, as a leader.

how: Peter's denial is read in churches during Holy Week, and in Christian art a rooster beside Peter recalls it, a reminder both of failure and of forgiveness.

p: art not thou also one of his disciples?
did I not see thee in the garden?

s: the first question comes from the girl who keeps the door.
John uses the same word for a charcoal fire again later in his Gospel
while Peter denies him, Jesus is naming witnesses inside
ask them which heard me, he tells the high priest.

games.q: you're Peter, standing at the fire. a servant girl looks at you and asks: aren't you one of his disciples? what do you say?
games.why: "He saith, I am not." in the garden Jesus said 'I am'; at the fire Peter says 'I am not', three times.

practice: Peter's fire was a comfort and a hiding place at once, so think gently about yours: the group you go along with, the joke you laugh at to fit in, the silence you keep when someone you love isn't there to defend themselves.
Don't scold yourself; just notice where you stand to stay warm. If you pray, bring that place to God honestly; if not, simply name it to yourself.

wordCard.voice: Anthrakia. The Greek word for the charcoal fire where Peter warmed himself and said, three times, I am not.

orig.note: Greek: a charcoal fire. John uses it here and again at 21:9.

carryVoice: Your line: warming himself. Peter's story isn't over yet, not by a long way. The fire will be back.
